title: We Don’t Get There Without You
author: Admired Leadership
summary: A follow-up to the previous day's post on recognition, this piece argues that leaders habitually reward the visible, initiative-taking performers while neglecting those who quietly build the foundation of team success. The author says great leaders deliberately correct that imbalance by naming the background contributors and telling them plainly that the team does not get there without them. The same inclusion extends to people who are ill, injured or otherwise absent, who should still be pulled into updates, planning and celebrations in some symbolic way. The claimed payoff is higher morale, commitment and engagement, and the closing point is that results are not sustained unless the whole team is recognized.
points: Praise tends to flow to the people out front, so leaders must intentionally look for the below-the-radar contributors.
A simple repeated message, that the team cannot succeed without someone, brings overlooked members into the circle of recognition.
Absent or sidelined members should still be included in updates and celebrations, even symbolically.
Recognizing the whole team, not just standouts, is what sustains results over the long run.
quotes: They make it a point to link the distinct contributions of team members to specific outcomes. Specificity in what is being recognized and how it contributed to discrete outcomes is much more motivational than generic expressions of work well done.

Those who take charge, operate with initiative, and drive assignments forward get the bulk of the praise and recognition from leaders. It only makes sense to focus on those out in front and who make things go.
They understand that their contributions often go unnoticed or draw less praise and recognition than they should. Their talented colleagues seem to get all the press and attention.
They announce that they are an integral part of the team’s success. They pull them into the circle of recognition. They don’t allow them to watch from the outside.

Pulling team members who contribute less into the center of recognition and team success builds team morale, commitment, and engagement. In the long run, leaders don’t sustain results unless the entire team is recognized for the contributions they make.
